summary: Defines a way for an access router to provide a shared key to a mobile node for protecting Fast Mobile IPv6 signaling, using Secure Neighbor Discovery (SEND). Fast Binding Updates must be secured to avoid certain attacks, and this gives the node and router a symmetric key to do so. The mobile node generates a public/private key pair for the exchange.

eli5.summary: Before two people can pass secret notes, they need to agree on a secret code. This describes how a router and a moving device safely agree on one, so no stranger can fake the notes.

subtitle: How a router hands a mobile device a shared key, using Secure Neighbor Discovery, so fast handover requests can be trusted.

tldr.problem: In Fast Mobile IPv6, a Fast Binding Update changes where traffic for a mobile node's old address goes. If the sender is not proven to own that address, an attacker can redirect a victim's traffic at will.
tldr.mechanism: The mobile node makes a fresh public/private key pair and sends the public key in a SEND-protected Router Solicitation for Proxy Advertisement. The access router encrypts a random shared handover key with it and returns it in the Proxy Router Advertisement.
tldr.outcome: Later, the mobile node uses the handover key to authenticate its Fast Binding Update, and the router finds the key by the node's previous care-of address.

today: RFC 5269 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on Fast Mobile IPv6 in RFC 5268 and on SEND in RFC 3971.

sections.title: The Problem: Authorizing a Fast Binding Update
sections.content:
In Fast Mobile IPv6 (FMIPv6), a mobile node (MN) that is changing access routers sends a Fast Binding Update (FBU) to its previous access router (AR). The FBU makes traffic for the MN's previous care-of address get tunneled to its new care-of address. Only a node authorized to claim the old address should be able to cause this, or an attacker can redirect a victim's traffic at will.

RFC 5269 defines a lightweight way for the AR to provision a shared handover key on the MN. The provisioning happens at some arbitrary time before handover, so it adds no overhead to the handover itself. When the handover comes, the MN computes a Message Authentication Code (MAC) on the FBU, and the AR uses the previous care-of address carried in the FBU to find the right key.
sections.eli5: If anyone could tell the post office to forward your mail somewhere else, thieves would do it. So the post office and you first agree on a secret password.

sections.title: SEND and Cryptographically Generated Addresses
sections.content:
SEND protects IPv6 Neighbor Discovery and last hop router discovery from threats that are generally easier to mount on wireless networks, where the link to the access point cannot be physically secured. It uses Cryptographically Generated Addresses (CGAs): a CGA is formed by hashing together the subnet prefix, a random nonce and an RSA public key, the CGA public key. Signing a message with the matching CGA private key proves that the sender may claim the address.

The handover key exchange is required to have SEND security. The source address of the messages is a CGA and they are signed with the CGA private key. That is how the AR checks that the MN is entitled to the address before it gives out a key. The handover encryption key pair is separate from the SEND key pair and from the handover key itself.
sections.eli5: A CGA is an address that has its owner's fingerprint baked into it, so only the real owner can sign a message from it.

sections.title: Provisioning the Handover Key
sections.content:
The MN first MUST generate a handover key encryption public/private key pair, using exactly the same algorithm and parameters as SEND. It can reuse the pair on different access routers but MUST NOT use it for any other encryption or for signing. The pair SHOULD be discarded after HKEPK-LIFETIME or HKEPK-HANDOVERS handovers, whichever comes first.

The MN then MUST send a Router Solicitation for Proxy Advertisement (RtSolPr) containing a Handover Key Request Option with the public key. The source is a CGA of the MN, the SEND CGA and Signature options are included, and a SEND Nonce MUST be included for anti-replay protection. The MN also sets the AT field to its preferred FBU authentication algorithm.

The AR MUST validate the RtSolPr with SEND. If validation fails, the AR MUST NOT provision a key and MUST NOT change any existing key record for that address, since the message may come from an attacker. If it passes, the AR returns the existing key if the CGA already has one. Otherwise it builds a new key, encrypts it with the MN's public key, and sends it in a Handover Key Reply Option on the Proxy Router Advertisement (PrRtAdv), together with the lifetime and the SEND nonce. The AR stores the key indexed by the CGA, with the algorithm type and lifetime.

The MN validates the PrRtAdv, checks that it was signed with the router's certified key (using the SEND certification path messages if needed), and drops it if not. It matches the nonce to find the right private key, decrypts the handover key, and stores it with the algorithm type and lifetime, indexed by the AR's address and its own CGA. Before the lifetime ends, the MN MUST request a new key if it still needs the service. The MN SHOULD NOT request a weaker algorithm than its original request, to prevent bidding-down attacks.
sections.eli5: The device makes a padlock and sends it, signed, to the router. The router puts a secret code in a box locked with that padlock. Only the device has the key to open it.

sections.title: Using the Key on an FBU
sections.content:
When the MN sends an FBU to the previous AR, it MUST use the handover key and the agreed algorithm to generate the authentication MAC and MUST include it in the message. It picks the key using the previous AR's address and its previous care-of CGA, and includes the old care-of CGA in a Home Address Option, as FMIPv6 defines.

The previous AR MUST look up the key using the care-of CGA in the Home Address Option and verify the authenticator with it. If no key is found, the AR MUST NOT change forwarding for that address.

The AR MUST generate a random key strong enough for the algorithm and a unique key per CGA public key. The previous AR SHOULD NOT discard a still-valid key right after use, because the MN may move again quickly. It MUST discard the key when forwarding for the previous care-of address times out or HK-LIFETIME expires. The MN SHOULD discard it once the Mobile IPv6 binding update is complete on the new AR, and MUST NOT assume it can keep using an old key without receiving it again.
sections.eli5: When the device moves, it signs its forwarding request with the secret code. The old router only obeys requests signed with the code it gave out.

sections.title: The Two Neighbor Discovery Options
sections.content:
Both new options are standard IPv6 Neighbor Discovery options in type-length-value form. The Handover Key Request Option (type 27) rides in the RtSolPr and holds the handover key encryption public key. The Handover Key Reply Option (type 28) rides in the PrRtAdv and holds the key lifetime in seconds and the shared key encrypted with RSAES-PKCS1-v1_5.

Both have a Length in units of 8 octets (the value 0 is invalid and the receiver MUST discard such a message), a Pad Length, a 4-bit AT field naming the FBU authentication algorithm, and a 4-bit reserved field set to zero. Padding makes the option a multiple of 8 octets. The request key MUST be formatted like the CGA key in the message and have the same parameters.
sections.eli5: These are two labeled slots in a message: one for the device's padlock and one for the locked box with the code.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
General CGA security considerations apply. The protocol carries the same replay and denial-of-service risks from the RtSolPr as SEND does for router solicitation, and the mitigations recommended in RFC 3971 apply here too.

To avoid state depletion attacks, the AR SHOULD NOT generate the handover key before SEND processing has verified the sender of the RtSolPr. Rate limiting RtSolPr, limiting the state held for unresolved solicitations and careful cache management are the techniques named, the same as for Neighbor Discovery.
sections.eli5: The router only makes a secret code after it has checked who is asking, so crooks cannot make it waste effort on fake requests.

sections.title: Constants and IANA
sections.content: The RFC suggests three defaults: HKEPK-LIFETIME of 12 hours, HKEPK-HANDOVERS of 10, and HK-LIFETIME of 12 hours (43200 seconds). IANA assigned Neighbor Discovery option type codes 27 for the Handover Key Request Option and 28 for the Handover Key Reply Option.
sections.eli5: The keys are meant to be thrown away after a half day, or after ten moves for the padlock.

messages.label: RtSolPr + Handover Key Request
messages.note: Carries the handover key encryption public key, signed with SEND.

messages.label: PrRtAdv + Handover Key Reply
messages.note: Carries the handover key encrypted with that public key, signed with SEND.

messages.label: FBU with MAC
messages.note: Authenticated with the handover key, sent to the previous AR at handover time.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Option length in units of 8 octets; 0 is invalid.

fields.name: Pad Length
fields.desc: Padding octets after the encrypted key.

fields.name: AT
fields.desc: Algorithm type for the FBU authenticator.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Zero on send, ignored on receipt.

fields.name: Key Lifetime
fields.desc: Lifetime of the handover key in seconds.
